name: Strategic pluralism (double-mating)

card.summary: An evolutionary-psychology theory that people flex between short-term and long-term mating tactics, with physical attractiveness acting as a key cue of genetic quality, which is why looks are discussed as a lever on mating outcomes.
card.note: A theoretical framework; effect sizes in tests are often small.

quick.overview:
Strategic pluralism, also called the dual-mating strategy, is a hypothesis proposed by Steven Gangestad and Jeffry Simpson in 2000. It holds that humans evolved conditional mating strategies, short-term and long-term, chosen according to cues about their own condition and circumstances.

For looksmaxxing, the theory matters because physical attractiveness, symmetry and masculine traits are treated as signals of genetic quality that people are said to weigh in mate choice. Community discussions use it to explain why looks can matter for dating, while research reports mixed and often small effects.
quick.how: It is a framework for understanding mating behaviour rather than a practice. People refer to it when discussing why attractiveness and status matter differently for short-term and long-term pairing.
quick.risks: There is no physical risk. The theory is debated in academia, and tests have found small effects, for instance a 2021 meta-analysis found men's self-rated mate value explains roughly 6% of variance in sociosexual orientation.

lead: Strategic pluralism is an evolutionary-psychology theory, formalised by Steven Gangestad and Jeffry Simpson in a 2000 Behavioral and Brain Sciences article, which argues that during human history there were trade-offs between time and energy spent on mating and on child-rearing. Both sexes therefore evolved conditional strategies guided by cues about circumstances [1].

In the theory's account, some men may succeed with many short-term matings, while others invest in one mate and her offspring, and women may favour men with features signalling genetic benefits to offspring in short-term contexts [1]. A Grokipedia summary adds that women are described as weighing genetic quality and provisioning, giving rise to the 'dual-mating' label, and that physical attractiveness and symmetry are treated as indicators of genetic quality [2].

For readers interested in appearance, this is the evolutionary basis on which attractiveness is argued to matter: looks are treated as a cue in mate choice, so improving them could shift the options available to a person.

chain: Theory treats attractiveness as a cue of genetic quality
Higher attractiveness predicted to widen short-term mating options
angle.text: The theory gives a rationale some communities use for why improving looks matters in dating. It is explanatory rather than a method for changing appearance.

paras: Robert Trivers' 1972 parental-investment theory says the sex that invests more in offspring is choosier, while the other sex competes for access [3]. Strategic pluralism builds on this, adding that individuals adjust tactics to circumstance and that mate value shapes which tactic suits them [2].
The theory proposes that short-term and long-term strategies trade off and that cues such as attractiveness, body symmetry and testosterone signal which strategy suits an individual [1][2].

A 2021 meta-analysis of 33 studies (N=5,928) found that men's self-reported mate value predicts less restricted sociosexual orientation, but accounts for only about 6% of the variance [4]. A 2022 study examined how socioeconomic status, protection skills and parenthood disposition relate to men's long-term mating orientation [5]. A 2006 paper examined sex similarities and differences in preferences for short-term mates [6]. Many other cited works concern insect sperm competition and are not about humans.

On forums, ideas such as double-mating are used to explain why women might prefer attractive men for short-term and reliable partners for long-term pairing. Discussions are widely dispersed, and the framework is contested by scholars.

timeline.event: Gangestad and Simpson publish strategic pluralism [1]
Meta-analysis finds small link between male mate value and short-term orientation [4]
